content: Vitamin A deficiency is a critical public health issue in many lowand middle-income countries, particularly affecting young children, women of reproductive age, and pregnant women. To address this, fortification of staple foods with vitamin A has been implemented as a strategy to increase vitamin A intake among these vulnerable groups. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of fortifying staple foods with vitamin A on reducing vitamin A deficiency and improving health-related outcomes in the general population aged over two years. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the fortification of staple foods such as sugar, edible oils, maize flour, wheat flour, milk, and condiments with vitamin A, either alone or in combination with other micronutrients. The studies included participants from any country, provided they were older than two years, including pregnant and lactating women. A total of 10 RCTs involving 4,455 participants were included in the review. These studies were conducted in lowand upper-middle-income countries where vitamin A deficiency is a public health concern. The interventions lasted between three and nine months. The studies were funded by government organizations, non-governmental organizations, private sectors, and academic institutions, and there was no evidence that the funding sources biased the results. Key Findings: 1. Staple Foods Fortified with Vitamin A Alone vs. Unfortified Foods: It is uncertain whether fortifying staple foods with vitamin A alone has any significant effect on serum retinol concentrations (mean difference [MD] 0.03 μmol/L, 95% confidence interval [CI] −0.06 to 0.12; 3 studies, 1,829 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is also uncertain regarding whether vitamin A fortification alone reduces the risk of subclinical vitamin A deficiency (risk ratio [RR] 0.45, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.05; 2 studies, 993 participants; very low-certainty evidence). There is uncertainty about whether vitamin A fortification reduces clinical vitamin A deficiency, such as night blindness (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.98; 1 study, 581 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The certainty of the evidence was affected by high risk of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency. 2. Staple Foods Fortified with Vitamin A Alone vs. No Intervention: No studies provided data for this comparison. 3. Staple Foods Fortified with Vitamin A Plus Other Micronutrients vs. Unfortified Foods: Fortifying staple foods with vitamin A plus other micronutrients may not significantly increase serum retinol concentrations (MD 0.08 μmol/L, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.22; 4 studies, 1,009 participants; low-certainty evidence). However, this intervention probably reduces the risk of subclinical vitamin A deficiency compared to unfortified foods (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.49; 3 studies, 923 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The certainty of the evidence was affected by serious risk of bias and inconsistency. 4. Staple Foods Fortified with Vitamin A Plus Other Micronutrients vs. No Intervention: Fortification with vitamin A plus other micronutrients may increase serum retinol concentrations (MD 0.22 μmol/L, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.30; 2 studies, 318 participants; low-certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether this intervention reduces the risk of subclinical vitamin A deficiency (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.98; 2 studies, 318 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The certainty of the evidence was affected by serious imprecision and risk of bias. 5. Other Outcomes: None of the included trials reported on outcomes such as all-cause morbidity, all-cause mortality, adverse effects, food intake, congenital anomalies (for pregnant women), or breast milk vitamin A concentrations (for lactating women). Conclusions: Fortifying staple foods with vitamin A alone may have little or no effect on serum retinol concentrations or the risk of subclinical vitamin A deficiency. When compared to unfortified foods, fortification with vitamin A plus other micronutrients may not significantly increase serum retinol concentrations but probably reduces the risk of subclinical vitamin A deficiency. Compared to no intervention, fortification with vitamin A plus other micronutrients may increase serum retinol concentrations, but it is uncertain whether it reduces the risk of subclinical vitamin A deficiency due to very low-certainty evidence. The effects of fortification on other health outcomes, such as mortality, morbidity, and adverse effects, remain unknown as no trials reported these outcomes. The funding sources for the studies did not appear to influence the results.
